content: Home residents need a DigitalHome system for monitoring and controlling devices that affect security, temperature, humidity, lighting, and small appliances. General users should be able to manage their home environment through a personal web interface, while designated master users and technicians need additional configuration capabilities. The system must coordinate information and commands between its web services and the sensors and controllers installed in the home.

We want it to help residents keep an eye on the home and control the main things that affect comfort and safety, especially security, temperature, humidity, lighting, and a few small appliances. In practical terms, people should be able to check conditions, react to alerts, and make changes remotely through their web interface.
The scope should cover normal day-to-day home management as well as unusual situations like a door or window being opened, a room getting too hot or humid, lights being left on, or a device needing to be switched off. It’s mainly about monitoring and control inside the home, with coordination between the web system and the devices installed there.

At the moment, those are the main ones we want to cover. I wouldn’t want to add more domains unless we find a clear need during design or from the users, because I’d rather keep the first version focused. If something else comes up later, we can consider it as an extension.

We’re mainly thinking about typical private residences like apartments and single-family homes. Shared homes could also be possible if the access and permissions are handled carefully, but that’s more of a maybe than a firm requirement right now. I don’t think we want to target commercial buildings or anything outside normal residential use.

A general resident should be able to see the current status of the home, get alerts when something important changes, and control the allowed devices from the web interface. That includes things like adjusting temperature or lighting settings, checking humidity, and turning certain appliances on or off if they’re permitted to do so. They should be able to do the day-to-day actions without needing help from a technician.

I’d keep those as out of scope for now unless we later decide there’s a strong need. Vacation rentals, dorms, and similar places usually have more complex access rules and operational constraints, so I’d rather not assume we support them in the first release. The safest scope is still ordinary residential homes where the users are more or less the occupants or owners.

A technician should be able to install, configure, and maintain the sensors and controllers, and also troubleshoot when a device or connection is not working correctly. They would need access to system settings that a normal resident should not see, especially anything related to pairing devices, calibration, and diagnostics. Residents should mainly use the system day to day, while technicians handle setup and repair.

I think we should keep a shared terminology in the system so everyone sees the same core names for devices, zones, and modes. That will reduce confusion, especially when technicians are configuring things and residents are using them later. We can still allow some friendly display names, but the underlying terms should stay consistent.

Friendly display names should be set by the master user or technician, since they’re the ones who understand the setup details. Those names can show up in the resident interface to make things easier to recognize, but the core terminology should still be visible in configuration and diagnostic areas. In logs, alerts, and technical screens, I’d prefer the core names to stay available so there’s no ambiguity.

It should explain the failure in plain language, not just give a code or a technical message. If possible, it should suggest the next practical step, like trying again, checking the device connection, or contacting the technician if the problem looks more serious. For residents, the message should stay simple, while technicians can see more detail for troubleshooting.

When a command is accepted, the interface should immediately show that it is in progress so the user knows the request went through. Then it should update to either a clear success confirmation or a rejection message if the system could not carry it out. I’d want that feedback to be quick and unambiguous, especially for things like security or temperature changes.

Manual commands should take priority, especially when a resident or master user is acting intentionally. If an automated rule gets overridden, the system should tell the user what happened so it’s clear why the device ended up in that state. For technicians, it would also be useful to see that conflict in the logs or status view.

I don’t have a firm retention period in mind yet. For normal day-to-day state, I’d expect the current values to stay available as long as the device is active, and the history should probably be kept long enough for troubleshooting and trends, but we’d need to verify the actual archive or deletion policy with the business team.

It should start with a technician or installer pairing the home devices to the DigitalHome system and assigning them to the right zones and functions. After that, the master user should be able to review the setup, name things, and confirm the basic rules or schedules before the home goes live. I’d want the process to be guided and fairly simple, because this is usually happening during installation, not as an ongoing admin task.

Technicians should be able to pair and remove devices, calibrate sensors, verify controller operation, and run diagnostics or connectivity checks. They should also be able to view technical status, logs, and error details, but not manage resident preferences, daily automation choices, or personal schedules. I’d draw the line so they can maintain the system, but not use it like a resident or change private household settings.

It should stop short of fully enrolling it and ask the installer to confirm the type, zone, or function manually. If the system is unsure, I’d rather it leave the device in a pending setup state than guess and put it in the wrong room or control category. For technicians, it should explain what was ambiguous so they can correct it quickly.

Yes, there should be some exclusions and limits. For example, certain rooms may be marked private or off-limits for automation, and some device types may only be monitored without being controlled, especially if the hardware is not certified for remote action. I’d also expect the system to suppress or reduce alerts in cases like maintenance mode, installation testing, or when a resident explicitly disables notifications for a period.

Those exclusions should normally be set by a master user, and technicians should only be able to apply or lift them temporarily while doing installation, maintenance, or troubleshooting. If a technician bypasses an exclusion, I’d want that to be time-limited, clearly logged, and visible to the master user afterward. For anything that changes long-term privacy or notification behavior, the technician shouldn’t be able to do it alone.

The home needs a stable local network with enough Wi‑Fi coverage or wired connectivity for the controllers and hub to stay online reliably. During installation, devices should be powered, reachable, and within range for pairing, and the environment shouldn’t have major interference or dead spots that would break sensor communication. If the network is weak, I’d expect the installer to flag it before finishing setup so it doesn’t become a support problem later.

At installation, the system should verify that the hub can reach the internet and the required DigitalHome web services, and that inbound or outbound connections aren’t blocked by the home network. It should also check that the hub can communicate with the in-home devices it’s supposed to manage, either directly or through the local controllers. If those checks fail, setup should pause or stay in a limited mode until the installer fixes the network path.

In practice, it should serve residents first, because the main purpose is day-to-day home management through their personal interface. Master users should get the extra coordination and configuration rights for household-wide settings, while technicians should only use that same context for setup and support, not to change resident routines. So residents control usage, master users control broader policy, and technicians stay limited to maintenance-related actions.

They should be allowed to pair devices, assign them to rooms or zones, test sensor and controller communication, and fix connectivity or calibration issues. They can also verify alert delivery and make temporary maintenance changes when needed. The boundary is that they shouldn’t be able to create or alter resident schedules, scenes, permissions, or long-term automation rules unless a master user explicitly authorizes that change.

Yes, the system should treat master user permissions as higher priority than technician actions, so a master user can always override a technician if there’s a conflict. If a resident is actively using a device, the technician’s maintenance action should be blocked or deferred unless it’s a safe diagnostic action that won’t disrupt operation. In practice, any simultaneous change should be resolved by locking the setting or prompting for approval, rather than letting both changes go through.

If both are touching the same setting, the system should default to the master user having immediate control and the technician being blocked or asked to wait. If the technician already has an active maintenance session, then the system should lock the setting for normal changes and require the master user to explicitly approve any override. I don’t think we’ve defined any case where the technician would win over the master user for that kind of change.

Yes, that would make sense. Residents should be able to change the friendly name they see in the home app, while the core device name used in configuration, logs, alerts, and diagnostics should be controlled by master users or technicians, depending on the kind of setup change. That way the everyday label can stay user-friendly without breaking the technical records.

For temperature and humidity, the system should alert when readings move outside preset safe ranges for a sustained period, and it can also trigger automatic control like HVAC, humidifier, or dehumidifier adjustments before it becomes a comfort issue. For security, it should react immediately to events like intrusion, forced entry, or tamper detection, with alerts going out right away and emergency escalation only for the most serious cases. Any automatic action should have a short delay or confirmation window only if it won’t reduce safety, and residents or master users should be able to override comfort-related actions, but not the security emergency response once it has been triggered.

For temperature and humidity, it should wait briefly and confirm the condition is still present before alerting or acting, so we don’t react to a one-off spike. If it clears and then comes back, the system can retry the check and only escalate if it stays out of range for a defined period. For security events, there should be almost no waiting; once confirmed, it should stay active until the sensor reports normal again and the system verifies that the alarm condition has genuinely ended.

Yes, there will almost certainly be some practical limits, but I don’t have a finalized list yet. I would expect the web interface to work on common modern browsers and the services to run on whatever home gateway or hosted backend we standardize on, but the exact supported hardware and OS versions still need to be verified. If there are any old devices or unusual browsers in scope, we’d need to call those out explicitly.

It should open with a very simple guided setup that shows the main areas first, like security, climate, lighting, and appliances, and explains what each one does in plain language. I’d also expect a quick tour or onboarding tips the first time they log in, with the option to skip it once they’re comfortable. The goal is that a new resident can understand the basics and start controlling the home without needing a manual.

Yes, they should be able to resume it later from a help or onboarding area. If they skip or close it, the system should immediately take them to the main home dashboard so they can use the controls right away, and the tour should simply be marked as incomplete rather than blocked. That way onboarding is optional, not a gate to basic use.

Yes, residents should not be shown misleading data. If a reading is stale, missing, or clearly out of range for the device, the dashboard should flag it rather than present it as normal, and if the system has an estimated value it should be labeled as such. For anything critical, like security, a stale or unavailable reading should be treated as an issue and surfaced prominently instead of hidden.

They should see a clear status for each command, starting with something like queued or sent, then in progress, then completed or failed. If it times out, gets rejected, or can’t reach the device, the message should say that plainly and ideally give a short reason, like device offline or command not supported. For anything that fails, the user should know whether they can retry immediately or need to wait.

For a normal sensor, I think the dashboard should keep the tile visible and show the last known value with a clear warning, or mark it as unavailable if there is no trustworthy value at all. I would not hide it completely, because residents need to know something is wrong, especially for security or climate devices. The only real difference by role would be that master users and technicians might see a bit more diagnostic detail, while general residents just see the warning and status.

My expectation is that private rooms should be visible only to the residents who are authorized for that space, and ordinary residents should not see or control devices in other people’s private rooms. For non-certified devices, I’d treat them more cautiously: they might be viewable in a limited way, but control should be restricted until they’re approved or registered properly. Master users could likely override some restrictions for administration, and technicians might need temporary access for maintenance, but that should be explicit and auditable.

Technicians should only get temporary access when there is a maintenance request, a fault, or a user-approved installation or repair, not for routine browsing. The access should be limited to the specific room or device, time-boxed to a short window, and it should expire automatically unless renewed by an authorized master user. While it’s active, the system should log who granted it, when it started and ended, what area or device was opened, and any commands or changes made.

In practice, I’d block remote control by default until the device is certified or explicitly approved. If the system can still detect it, it should probably stay visible in a limited, view-only state so residents and staff know it exists and can see status, but the control buttons should be disabled with a reason. Hiding it entirely would make troubleshooting harder, so I’d prefer limited visibility over full concealment.

During installation testing, the system should open up only the parts needed to verify setup, but it should still protect resident privacy as much as possible. Technicians and master users may need broader visibility and control for the devices being tested, while ordinary residents should see that something is under installation but not be exposed to unnecessary details or controls. Once testing is finished, everything should return to normal access rules automatically.

I’d keep that fairly short, probably on the order of a few hours at most, because it should only cover the active installation session. If the work is still going on after that, it should have to be renewed explicitly by an authorized master user or by whatever installation workflow we use. I don’t know the exact number yet, but I’d lean toward a same-day limit rather than anything open-ended.

That renewal should require a master user, not the technician themselves. Technicians can request it, but the approval should come from someone with household authority or from a designated administrator in the setup process.

Yes, it should be blocked or at least deferred if a resident is actively using the device and the action would interrupt something important, like heating, lighting, or security behavior. It should also be deferred if another approved maintenance or configuration change is already in progress on the same device, because we don’t want conflicting commands. In those cases, the system should tell the technician why it’s being held and let a master user decide if it can proceed urgently.

If someone isn’t authorized, they should be blocked from viewing the room’s details and from sending any control commands to devices in that space. They shouldn’t be able to infer too much either, beyond maybe a generic access denied message, because private rooms should stay private. A master user or technician can have temporary access only when there’s a clear operational need, like maintenance, installation, or an emergency, and that access should be time-limited and logged.

A valid operational need would be things like repairing a faulty sensor, replacing a controller, commissioning a new device, or handling an urgent safety issue such as a smoke, temperature, or security alarm. Even then, the access should be narrowed to just the affected room or device and only for the time needed. It should still be refused if the request is unrelated to the issue, too broad, or if granting it would create a clear privacy risk that isn’t justified by the emergency.

It shouldn’t automatically repeat every time someone logs in again after the first use. If they’ve already completed onboarding, they should normally go straight to the main interface, but we could show the tour again if the user explicitly asks for help or if there’s been a major interface change.

Yes, the explanations should adapt a bit based on user type. A general resident should see simple wording focused on what they can control, while a master user or technician can get a little more detail about configuration and maintenance functions. If a home doesn’t have a certain feature or device yet, that area should either be hidden or shown as unavailable so we don’t explain controls that don’t exist.

For master users, onboarding should cover things like adding or removing devices, setting room mappings, changing automation rules, and reviewing alerts or access logs. For technicians, it should focus more on installation, calibration, diagnostics, and device replacement or commissioning rather than household policy settings. Even with those roles, some details should still be limited if they’re outside that person’s assigned scope or if exposing them would reveal unrelated private-room information.

It should use the user’s role and permissions to decide what content to show, so the tour only includes rooms, devices, and functions they’re actually allowed to access. If there are hidden or restricted areas, onboarding should not mention them at all, because we don’t want to reveal that they exist. The level of detail should stay simple for regular residents and more technical only for master users or technicians, but still limited to their authorized scope.

I don’t have the exact version numbers decided yet, so I’d need to verify that with the team. In practice, we’d usually define a current supported range for common modern browsers and recent phone/tablet operating systems, and then explicitly exclude very old versions that can’t handle the interface reliably. If there are any legacy devices in the homes we already know about, those would need to be called out separately.
